cards.front: Why can a single chemoreceptor cell not tell the brain which molecule activated it?
cards.back: Its output is only how strongly it is active. Different molecules can drive it equally, so a chemical sense can tell stimuli apart only by their patterns across separate lines.
cards.quote: A receptor cell reports only how strongly it is active, not which molecule activated it.
cards.section: One coding problem, two answers

cards.front: In chemical-sense coding, a {{c1::line}} is a set of cells whose activity reaches the brain as one channel.
cards.back: In smell: all neurons expressing one receptor, plus their glomeruli. In taste: one kind of receptor cell.
cards.quote: A line is a set of cells whose activity reaches the brain as one channel.
cards.section: One coding problem, two answers

cards.front: A line whose activity always means one quality, whatever turned it on, is called a {{c1::labeled line}}.
cards.quote: A line whose activity always means one quality, whatever turned it on, is called a labeled line.
cards.section: One coding problem, two answers

cards.front: How does the principle of univariance in vision express the same limit as a chemoreceptor cell's output?
cards.back: A cone's response cannot say whether it met a dim light at its best wavelength or a brighter light far from it, just as a receptor cell reports strength, not identity.
cards.quote: In vision it is the principle of univariance: a cone's response cannot say whether it met a dim light at the wavelength it is most sensitive to
cards.section: One coding problem, two answers

cards.front: Odorant receptors are {{c1::G-protein-coupled receptors}}, with seven transmembrane segments.
cards.back: The family has roughly a thousand genes in the mouse and a few hundred intact genes in humans.
cards.quote: The receptors are G-protein-coupled receptors, with seven transmembrane segments.
cards.section: Smell keeps its lines apart

cards.front: Where do the axons of olfactory sensory neurons end, and onto which cells?
cards.back: In glomeruli of the olfactory bulb, where they meet the dendrites of the bulb's output neurons, the mitral and tufted cells.
cards.quote: where receptor-neuron axons meet the dendrites of the bulb's output neurons, the mitral and tufted cells.
cards.section: Smell keeps its lines apart

cards.front: Most mature mouse olfactory neurons express one odorant-receptor gene. Why can such a neuron still respond to several odorants, and what does the one-gene rule fix?
cards.back: Its single receptor can bind several odorants: the rule is about genes, not odorants. It fixes that each neuron speaks for one receptor type, so neurons sharing a receptor form one line.
cards.quote: One receptor per neuron is a statement about genes, not about odorants
cards.section: Smell keeps its lines apart

cards.front: Mice were engineered so that olfactory neurons expressing one chosen receptor also filled their axons with a marker. What did the labelled axons show?
cards.back: The cell bodies were scattered across the epithelium, but their axons converged on two fixed glomeruli out of about 1,800 per bulb. Each glomerulus collects mainly from one receptor type.
cards.why: So the glomerular layer is largely a map of lines: receptor identity laid out as position.
cards.quote: and they end in two fixed glomeruli out of the roughly 1,800 in each bulb
cards.section: Smell keeps its lines apart

cards.front: In mice, the coding sequence of odorant receptor P2 was replaced with that of receptor M12. The axons went to new glomeruli, distinct from both P2's and M12's usual targets. What does this show about how axons choose a glomerulus?
cards.back: The receptor helps guide its own axon, since changing it moved the axons. It is probably not the only cue, since the swapped-in receptor did not carry the axons to M12's site.
cards.quote: the receptor helps guide its own axon but is probably not the only cue
cards.section: Smell keeps its lines apart

cards.front: In a canonical olfactory neuron, what is the transduction sequence from the bound receptor to depolarization?
cards.back: Receptor activates Golf, which drives adenylyl cyclase 3 to make cAMP. cAMP opens cyclic-nucleotide-gated channels that admit Na+ and Ca2+; a calcium-activated chloride current amplifies the depolarization.
cards.quote: The bound receptor activates the G protein Golf, which drives adenylyl cyclase 3 to make cAMP.
cards.section: Smell keeps its lines apart

cards.front: Every canonical olfactory neuron uses the same Golf-cAMP cascade, whatever its receptor. Why does this not erase odour identity?
cards.back: The shared cascade attaches no chemical name to the response. Which odorant arrived is carried by the pattern of response strengths across lines (timing can contribute in real neurons).
cards.quote: Because the cascade is shared, it does not attach a chemical name to the response.
cards.section: Smell keeps its lines apart

cards.front: Dissociated mouse olfactory neurons were loaded with a calcium indicator and exposed to a panel of odorants, and each responding cell's receptor was identified by single-cell RT-PCR. What three findings did the receptor-by-odorant grid show?
cards.back: One receptor recognized several odorants. One odorant was recognized by several receptors. Changing an odorant's concentration could change which receptors it activated.
cards.quote: One receptor recognized several odorants. One odorant was recognized by several receptors.
cards.section: Reading the pattern

cards.front: In olfaction, odour identity is a {{c1::combinatorial code}}: a pattern across receptors rather than one receptor per odour.
cards.quote: Odour identity, on this view, is a combinatorial code: a pattern across receptors rather than one receptor per odour.
cards.section: Reading the pattern

cards.front: Two odorants activate exactly the same set of mouse olfactory receptors. Can the animal's periphery still tell them apart, and why?
cards.back: Yes, if the relative strengths differ. Real responses are graded, and a pattern is the relative strength of activity across lines, not just which lines are on.
cards.quote: Real responses are graded, so two odorants that activate the same set of receptors can still be told apart if the relative strengths differ.
cards.section: Reading the pattern

cards.front: Invented mouse receptor data (on or off): odorant 1 activates A+B, odorant 2 B+C, odorant 3 A+B+C, odorant 4 D. Odorants can be told apart only if their patterns differ. Receptor C is removed. Which odorants can no longer be told apart, and why?
cards.back: Odorants 1 and 3. Without C, odorant 1 is A+B, odorant 2 is B, odorant 3 is A+B and odorant 4 is D. Only the distinction that rested on C is lost.
cards.quote: Losing a line costs only the distinctions that depended on it.
cards.section: Reading the pattern

cards.front: In the simplified line model, one receptor-defined line is silenced and the other lines are unchanged. Which glomeruli lose that line's activity, and which odour discriminations does the model predict will suffer?
cards.back: Mainly the roughly two glomeruli per bulb that collect from that receptor's line. Only odorants whose remaining patterns become identical lose their distinction; those whose remaining patterns differ stay distinguishable. This is a model prediction, not the anatomical or behavioural result of a gene knockout.
cards.why: Combines convergence (each glomerulus collects mainly from one receptor type) with the matrix rule that losing a line costs only the distinctions that depended on it.
cards.quote: Assume the brain can tell two odorants apart only if their patterns differ.
cards.section: Reading the pattern

cards.front: Invented mouse receptor data, all receptors present: odorant 1 = A+B, 2 = B+C, 3 = A+B+C, 4 = D. Receptor C has low affinity for odorant 1 and is recruited only when odorant 1 is raised tenfold. What happens to odorant 1's identity, and why?
cards.back: Its pattern becomes A+B+C, matching odorant 3's low-concentration pattern, so the model predicts it could be mistaken for odorant 3: quality changes with concentration.
cards.why: C needs more odorant to reach its response threshold, so the stronger stimulus recruits an extra line.
cards.quote: The model predicts that odorant 1 at high concentration could be mistaken for odorant 3
cards.section: Reading the pattern

cards.front: Treat each of 8 olfactory receptor types as a switch that is either on or off. How many distinct non-empty activity patterns are possible?
cards.back: Patterns = 2^N − 1 = 2^8 − 1 = 256 − 1 = 255. The −1 removes the all-off pattern, which reports no odorant.
cards.why: This is the capacity of a toy model, not a count of smells: real responses are graded and noisy, and the bulb and cortex transform the pattern.
cards.quote: number of distinct non-empty patterns = 2^N − 1
cards.section: Reading the pattern

cards.front: Trace the central taste pathway from the cranial nerves to cortex.
cards.back: Cranial nerves VII, IX and X → nucleus of the solitary tract (medulla) → thalamus (in rodents via the parabrachial nucleus) → gustatory cortex in the insula.
cards.quote: Afferent fibres of cranial nerves VII, IX and X carry their signals to the nucleus of the solitary tract in the medulla
cards.section: Taste pools its receptors into cells

cards.front: Is there a tongue map with sweet at the tip and bitter at the back?
cards.back: No. That textbook map is discredited: taste buds across the tongue detect every quality, with only modest regional differences in sensitivity.
cards.quote: taste buds across the tongue detect every quality, with modest regional differences in sensitivity
cards.section: Taste pools its receptors into cells

cards.front: Sweet taste cells carry one main receptor, the pair {{c1::T1R2 and T1R3}}.
cards.back: They are type II cells, and the receptor is G-protein-coupled.
cards.quote: Sweet cells carry one main receptor, the pair T1R2 and T1R3.
cards.section: Taste pools its receptors into cells

cards.front: Umami taste cells carry {{c1::T1R1}} with T1R3; in mice this pair responds to many L-amino acids.
cards.quote: Umami cells carry T1R1 with T1R3; in mice this pair responds to many L-amino acids
cards.section: Taste pools its receptors into cells

cards.front: Which receptor family do bitter taste cells use, and how are the receptors distributed among rodent bitter cells?
cards.back: The T2R family (about 25 in humans, roughly 35 in mice). In rodents a single bitter cell expresses many T2Rs at once.
cards.quote: in rodents a single bitter cell expresses many T2Rs at once
cards.section: Taste pools its receptors into cells

cards.front: Why does taste have far fewer lines than smell?
cards.back: Partly because it has fewer receptor genes, but mainly because it pools them: receptors are sorted into a few kinds of cell, and each kind of cell is one line.
cards.quote: Taste has far fewer lines than smell, partly because it has fewer receptor genes but mainly because it pools them.
cards.section: Taste pools its receptors into cells

cards.front: In a mouse type II taste cell, what happens after PLCβ2 makes IP3?
cards.back: IP3 opens IP3R3 channels, releasing Ca2+ from the endoplasmic reticulum. Ca2+ opens TRPM5, which passes monovalent cations (Na+ and K+), so the cell depolarizes; TRPM4 contributes in mice.
cards.quote: calcium opens TRPM5, a channel gated by calcium that passes monovalent cations, sodium and potassium, so the cell depolarizes
cards.section: Taste pools its receptors into cells

cards.front: Mouse type II taste cells (sweet, umami, bitter) have no conventional vesicular synapse. How does their depolarization reach the afferent fibre?
cards.back: Depolarization opens CALHM1/3, a voltage-gated channel, and ATP flows out through it onto the afferent nerve fibres.
cards.quote: depolarization opens CALHM1/3, a voltage-gated channel, and ATP flows out through it onto the afferent nerve fibres
cards.section: Taste pools its receptors into cells

cards.front: Sweet and bitter type II taste cells use the same cascade and release the same transmitter. What keeps sweet and bitter apart?
cards.back: Which cell the nerve fibre listens to. A cell reports how strongly it is active, not what activated it, so the cell's identity, not the cascade, sets the quality.
cards.quote: So the cascade does not need to differ: what differs is which cell the nerve fibre listens to.
cards.section: Taste pools its receptors into cells

cards.front: PLCβ2 is deleted from the whole mouse. Which taste responses are lost and which remain, and why?
cards.back: In the reported mouse experiment, nerve responses to the tested sweet, amino-acid and bitter stimuli were lost. In lick tests, preference for sweet and amino acids was strongly reduced and bitter avoidance was lost. Sour and salty responses remained, because those cells use other routes.
cards.quote: Sour and salty responses remained, because those cells use other routes.
cards.section: Taste pools its receptors into cells

cards.front: In PLCβ2-knockout mice, PLCβ2 is restored only in taste cells that express T2R bitter receptors. Predict which taste responses return, and explain.
cards.back: Bitter only, in the nerve and in lick behaviour; sweet and amino-acid responses stay absent. The shared enzyme works only for the quality of the cell it sits in, so each cell type is a separate line.
cards.quote: The enzyme is shared, but it works only for the quality of the cell it sits in.
cards.section: Taste pools its receptors into cells

cards.front: Restoring PLCβ2 only in mouse bitter cells shows that taste lines are separate. What does it not show, and what kind of experiment would?
cards.back: It does not show that the cell, rather than the receptor, decides what the line means. That needs a receptor expressed in the wrong cell (ectopic expression).
cards.quote: It does not yet show that the cell, rather than the receptor, decides what the line means.
cards.section: Taste pools its receptors into cells

cards.front: A human bitter receptor, T2R16, is expressed in mouse sweet cells. Normal mice ignore its bitter ligand at the concentrations tested. Do the engineered mice avoid, drink or ignore the ligand, and why?
cards.back: They drink it: they become attracted to the bitter ligand. The receptor detected the molecule, but the sweet cell decided what the detection meant.
cards.quote: The receptor detected the molecule, but the sweet cell decided what the detection meant.
cards.section: Taste pools its receptors into cells

cards.front: Suppose a receptor activated only by a synthetic drug that mice otherwise ignore were expressed only in mouse umami (T1R1/T1R3) cells. Reasoning from the mouse taste results, predict the lick response to the drug.
cards.back: Attraction, as to amino acids. Each kind of mouse taste cell acts as a labeled line: its activity means one quality, whatever turned it on, so the umami cell would set the meaning.
cards.why: Extrapolates from the sweet-cell and bitter-cell experiments; the umami case itself is not reported.
cards.quote: In this sense each kind of taste cell acts as a labeled line in the mouse periphery
cards.section: Taste pools its receptors into cells

cards.front: Two different bitter compounds, each at a concentration that activates one rodent bitter cell equally, reach that cell. What can the brain learn from the cell's firing rate?
cards.back: Only how strongly the cell was activated, not which compound it met: both send the same signal, because the cell pools many T2Rs.
cards.why: Not every bitter cell need carry the same T2Rs, so the pathway as a whole may keep some distinctions. Pooling fits a sense that mostly answers eat it or reject it.
cards.quote: Two different bitter compounds, each at a concentration that activates the cell equally, send the same signal from that cell.
cards.section: Taste pools its receptors into cells

cards.front: Which mouse taste cell type detects sour, and what is its acid sensor?
cards.back: Type III cells. Their sensor is OTOP1, a proton-selective channel.
cards.why: PKD2L1, long used to mark sour cells, is not the primary sour receptor.
cards.quote: Their acid sensor is OTOP1, a proton-selective channel identified by Tu and colleagues in 2018.
cards.section: Sour and salt: the channel routes

cards.front: How does transmitter release from mouse type III (sour) taste cells differ from that of type II cells?
cards.back: Type III cells form conventional synapses and release amine transmitters such as serotonin by calcium-dependent exocytosis. Type II cells have no vesicular synapse and release ATP through CALHM1/3.
cards.quote: They form conventional synapses, releasing amine transmitters such as serotonin by calcium-dependent exocytosis
cards.section: Sour and salt: the channel routes

cards.front: Mice lacking the taste nerve's ATP receptors, P2X2 and P2X3, lose taste nerve responses to every quality, including sour. What does that imply about serotonin as the sour cells' signal?
cards.back: Serotonin is probably not their only signal: if it were, sour responses should survive loss of the ATP receptors. ATP signalling is needed for sour as well.
cards.quote: serotonin is probably not their only signal, since mice lacking the nerve's ATP receptors, P2X2 and P2X3, lose taste nerve responses to every quality
cards.section: Sour and salt: the channel routes

cards.front: OTOP1 is expressed in mouse sweet cells, and those cells now respond to sour stimuli. What does this result establish, and what does it not?
cards.back: OTOP1 can make a cell respond to acid. It is a result about the cells, not about what the mice tasted; that needs nerve and behavioural tests.
cards.quote: a result about the cells, not about what the mice tasted
cards.section: Sour and salt: the channel routes

cards.front: Otop1-null mice lose OTOP1 proton currents and most of their taste nerve response to acid, yet still avoid acid in two-bottle tests. What does this say about avoidance as a measure of sour taste?
cards.back: Avoidance is not a pure measure of sour taste: acid can be avoided by routes outside OTOP1-based sour taste. Some acid sensitivity also remained, so sour-cell activity was not shown to be absent.
cards.quote: so avoidance is not a pure measure of sour taste
cards.section: Sour and salt: the channel routes

cards.front: What evidence ties mouse attraction to low salt to the epithelial sodium channel ENaC?
cards.back: Deleting the ENaCα subunit from taste cells abolished the amiloride-sensitive response to low sodium and the mice's attraction to low salt.
cards.quote: abolished the amiloride-sensitive response (the part blocked by the drug amiloride) to low sodium concentrations and the mice's attraction to low salt
cards.section: Sour and salt: the channel routes

cards.front: In a mouse with ENaC intact, which taste cell classes do high NaCl and a non-sodium salt such as KCl each drive?
cards.back: High NaCl drives ENaC sodium cells plus sour and bitter cells, two aversive pathways. KCl recruits the aversive pathways without the sodium-selective ENaC pathway.
cards.why: One stimulus driving several lines is a multi-line pattern, which the rule allows. This is a simplified account.
cards.quote: Non-sodium salts such as KCl recruit the aversive pathways without the sodium-selective ENaC pathway.
cards.section: Sour and salt: the channel routes

cards.front: A mouse lacks ENaCα in its taste cells. Using the cell-class account of mouse salt taste, predict its responses to low NaCl and to high NaCl.
cards.back: Low NaCl: the amiloride-sensitive response and attraction are lost. High NaCl: the lesson does not report this mutant. High NaCl also recruits sour and bitter cells as aversive pathways, so avoidance could plausibly persist if those routes remain functional and sufficient, but that is an extrapolation.
cards.why: Rests on high NaCl recruiting sour and bitter cells as aversive pathways separate from ENaC in ENaC-intact mice; the mutant's high-salt behaviour is not established.
cards.quote: High NaCl, which mice avoid, also recruited sour and bitter cells (Oka and colleagues, 2013).
cards.section: Sour and salt: the channel routes

cards.front: Contrast how smell and taste read quality at the periphery.
cards.back: Smell reads quality from a pattern across a large, overlapping receptor array, suited to an open-ended world of molecules. Taste reads it mainly from which cell class fires, a labeled line answering a few questions.
cards.quote: Taste mostly answers a few questions (eat it or reject it, and what it contains) with cells dedicated to each quality
cards.section: Back to the puzzles, and where the rule stops

cards.front: What evidence limits the labeled-line view of taste coding?
cards.back: Some taste cells and taste ganglion neurons respond to several qualities, and one stimulus such as high NaCl drives several cell classes. Labeled lines versus across-fibre patterns, especially further into the brain, is still argued.
cards.quote: Some taste cells and some taste ganglion neurons respond to several qualities
cards.section: Back to the puzzles, and where the rule stops

cards.front: Mice have dozens of bitter-receptor genes yet one bitter taste, while about a thousand odorant receptors yield many distinguishable odours. Explain the difference with one rule.
cards.back: A receptor cell reports only how strongly it is active. Bitter cells pool many T2Rs and signal one quality whatever receptor fired, so bitter is one line. Smell keeps each receptor type on its own line, so odours are read as patterns.
cards.quote: And bitter can be one taste because bitter cells signal one quality whatever receptor fired, and each pools many bitter receptors.
cards.section: Back to the puzzles, and where the rule stops

cards.front: Imagine every mouse olfactory neuron expressed many odorant receptors at once, as a rodent bitter cell pools many T2Rs. Predict the effect on odour discrimination.
cards.back: Pooling would make each cell's activity ambiguous about which of its ligands arrived, as with a bitter cell. But the premise alone does not give one effective line: different receptor subsets in different cells could still keep different patterns. Only if every neuron pooled the same receptors would odorants giving equal activity be indistinguishable.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that discrimination needs different patterns across separate lines, and on the bitter-pooling case, where not every bitter cell need carry the same T2Rs.
cards.quote: Smell keeps each receptor type on its own line, because most mature neurons express one receptor gene and like axons converge on about two glomeruli per bulb
cards.section: Back to the puzzles, and where the rule stops

cards.front: A receptor activated only by a synthetic drug is expressed only in mouse sweet cells, and the drug is tested in brief-access lick tests. Name the key controls and the main limit of the conclusion.
cards.back: Controls: confirm the receptor is only in the targeted cells (in situ hybridization or antibody staining); record the chorda tympani to show the drug drives a response; test wild-type littermates, which should ignore the drug; run a concentration series. Limit: mouse periphery only, and licking is a behaviour, not a reported percept.
cards.quote: Licking is a behaviour, not a reported percept, and brain circuits could in principle re-sort the signal.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A single TRPM5 channel has a unitary conductance of 25 pS, a linear current-voltage relation and a reversal potential of 0 mV. Taking outward current as positive, what is its current at a membrane potential of −40 mV?
cards.back: I = g × (Vm − Erev) = 25 pS × (−40 mV − 0 mV) = −1,000 fA = −1.0 pA. The minus sign means inward current of positive charge.
cards.why: A stipulated example, not a measured taste-cell current.
cards.quote: Then I = g × (Vm − Erev) = 25 pS × (−60 mV − 0 mV) = −1,500 fA = −1.5 pA.
cards.section: Worked problem: one TRPM5 channel
